stem: For a rare-procedure claim, the drafting agent is run five times independently. Three drafts approve coverage and two deny it, each citing a different clause of the ambiguous policy text. Both a wrong denial and a wrong payment are costly. What should the system do?

options.text: Accept the majority and approve the claim, since the most common answer across samples is the most reliable one
Resample the drafting agent until all runs agree, then accept the unanimous result as verified
Deny by default to protect plan funds, since an unresolved split means the claim is not clearly covered
Treat the split as an uncertainty signal and route the claim to a human adjudicator together with both readings and the clauses each one cites

explanation.why_correct: A 3-to-2 split is exactly the kind of scattered vote that self-consistency treats as low confidence rather than as a winner. With high costs on both sides of the error, the right move is selective abstention: withhold the automated decision and hand off an actionable package (competing readings plus cited clauses) so the human resolves the genuine ambiguity in the policy text.

why_incorrect.A: Majority voting helps when consensus is strong. A narrow 3-to-2 split on ambiguous wording carries little evidence, and acting on it automatically accepts a large chance of a costly error.
why_incorrect.B: Resampling until the runs agree manufactures consensus by selection and hides the underlying ambiguity. Agreement reached this way is not evidence of correctness.
why_incorrect.C: A default denial just converts uncertainty into a systematic harm to members. Abstention should escalate with next steps, not silently pick the outcome that is cheapest for the insurer.

explanation.rule_of_thumb: A split vote on a high-stakes decision is a signal to escalate with context, not a tie to be broken by the system itself.
